meta.title: Genetics: The Code That Builds You

plan.title: Genetics: The Code That Builds You
plan.hook: Your genome is a text written in four letters, read by machinery that turns genes into proteins, shuffled every generation — and now readable, and even editable, by us.
objectives: Pair the DNA bases correctly and describe DNA as information stored in base pairs
Trace the central dogma from DNA through RNA to protein and on to traits
Predict genotype and phenotype ratios for an Aa × Aa cross under complete dominance
Name the three mechanisms the course gives for genetic variation and what each one changes
Distinguish sequencing from editing: observing the code versus intervening at a target
prerequisites: Middle-school science: cells and the idea of inherited traits

sections.heading: DNA: The Code of Life
points: DNA stores information in base pairs
A pairs with T; C pairs with G
Two sugar-phosphate backbones hold the complementary base pairs

sections.heading: From Gene to Trait: The Central Dogma
points: DNA is transcribed to RNA; RNA is translated to protein
The protein is a chain of amino acids built from the RNA message
Proteins help produce traits — this simplified path is the central dogma

sections.heading: Inheritance: Mendel's Rules
points: Each parent contributes one allele per gene to the offspring
An Aa × Aa cross yields a genotype ratio of 1:2:1
Under complete dominance the phenotype ratio is 3:1

sections.heading: Where variation comes from
points: Mutation changes a base in the DNA sequence
Crossing over exchanges DNA between homologous chromosomes
Independent assortment shuffles chromosomes — together the three create genetic variation

sections.heading: Genetics in the Wild
points: Sequencing reads the order of DNA bases — it observes
Editing aims to change a chosen target — it intervenes
Reading a sequence is different from editing it

sections.heading: DNA: The Code of Life
sections.body: DNA stores information in base pairs. A pairs with T; C pairs with G.
sections.visual: The two sugar-phosphate backbones hold complementary base pairs: A with T, C with G.

questions.q: Which bases pair with each other in DNA?
questions.hint: Two pairings cover all four letters.
questions.answer: A pairs with T, and C pairs with G. The two sugar-phosphate backbones hold these complementary base pairs, and their order stores the information.

questions.q: Where is the information in a DNA molecule kept?
questions.hint: Not in the backbones — in what they hold in order.
questions.answer: In the sequence of base pairs. DNA stores information in base pairs, held in order between the two sugar-phosphate backbones.

sections.heading: From Gene to Trait: The Central Dogma
sections.body: DNA is transcribed to RNA; RNA is translated to protein. Proteins help produce traits.
sections.visual: In this simplified path, a gene is transcribed into message RNA, then translated into a chain of amino acids.
sections.diagram: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 400" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="DNA → RNA → protein"><title>DNA → RNA → protein</title><rect x="0" y="0" width="800" height="400" rx="16" fill="#101923"/><text x="28" y="35" fill="#e8ecf1" font-size="21" font-family="sans-serif">DNA → RNA → protein</text><path d="M28 51 L772 51" fill="none" stroke="#344253" stroke-width="2"/><text x="120" y="180" fill="#7cc7ff" font-size="20">DNA</text><path d="M180 170 L280 170" stroke="#7ee2a8" stroke-width="3" class="lw-flow"/><text x="320" y="180" fill="#7ee2a8" font-size="20">RNA</text><path d="M380 170 L480 170" stroke="#ffd479" stroke-width="3" class="lw-flow"/><circle class="lw-dogma-particle" cx="230" cy="170" r="6" fill="#ffd479"/><text x="520" y="180" fill="#ffd479" font-size="20">Protein</text><text class="lw-aa" x="600" y="220" fill="#b39dff" font-size="16">amino acids</text><path d="M28 350 L772 350" fill="none" stroke="#344253" stroke-width="2"/><text x="28" y="379" fill="#9aa6b8" font-size="15">Simplified eukaryotic gene expression</text></svg>

questions.q: What are the two steps from gene to protein, in order?
questions.hint: One rewrites the message; the other builds from it.
questions.answer: Transcription, then translation: DNA is transcribed to RNA, and RNA is translated to protein — a chain of amino acids.

questions.q: How do proteins connect to traits?
questions.hint: The body gives proteins the final role in the path.
questions.answer: Proteins help produce traits. The simplified path runs DNA → RNA → protein → trait.

sections.heading: Inheritance: Mendel's Rules
sections.body: An Aa × Aa cross yields genotype ratio 1:2:1 and phenotype ratio 3:1 under complete dominance.
sections.visual: Each cell combines one allele from each parent. Genotype ratio 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa.
sections.diagram: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 400" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Punnett square"><title>Punnett square</title><rect x="0" y="0" width="800" height="400" rx="16" fill="#101923"/><text x="28" y="35" fill="#e8ecf1" font-size="21" font-family="sans-serif">Aa × Aa outcomes</text><path d="M28 51 L772 51" fill="none" stroke="#344253" stroke-width="2"/><text class="lw-gamete" x="278" y="120" fill="#7cc7ff" font-size="20" text-anchor="middle">A</text><text class="lw-gamete" x="393" y="120" fill="#7cc7ff" font-size="20" text-anchor="middle">a</text><text class="lw-gamete" x="196" y="185" fill="#7cc7ff" font-size="20" text-anchor="middle">A</text><text class="lw-gamete" x="196" y="268" fill="#7cc7ff" font-size="20" text-anchor="middle">a</text><rect class="lw-punnett-cell" x="220" y="139" width="115" height="83" fill="#172331" stroke="#7ee2a8" stroke-width="2"/><text x="277" y="190" fill="#7ee2a8" font-size="28" text-anchor="middle">AA</text><rect class="lw-punnett-cell" x="335" y="139" width="115" height="83" fill="#172331" stroke="#7ee2a8" stroke-width="2"/><text x="392" y="190" fill="#7ee2a8" font-size="28" text-anchor="middle">Aa</text><rect class="lw-punnett-cell" x="220" y="222" width="115" height="83" fill="#172331" stroke="#7ee2a8" stroke-width="2"/><text x="277" y="273" fill="#7ee2a8" font-size="28" text-anchor="middle">Aa</text><rect class="lw-punnett-cell" x="335" y="222" width="115" height="83" fill="#172331" stroke="#b39dff" stroke-width="2"/><text x="392" y="273" fill="#b39dff" font-size="28" text-anchor="middle">aa</text><path d="M28 350 L772 350" fill="none" stroke="#344253" stroke-width="2"/><text x="28" y="379" fill="#9aa6b8" font-size="15">1:2:1 genotypes · 3:1 phenotypes</text></svg>

questions.q: What genotype and phenotype ratios does an Aa × Aa cross give?
questions.hint: Two ratios — one counts allele combinations, the other counts appearances.
questions.answer: Genotypes run 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa, and under complete dominance phenotypes run 3:1, because AA and Aa share the dominant phenotype.

questions.q: Where does each allele in an offspring's genotype come from?
questions.hint: The visual splits the contribution between the parents.
questions.answer: One allele comes from each parent: each cell in the Punnett square combines one allele from one parent with one from the other.

sections.heading: Where variation comes from
sections.body: Mutation, independent assortment, and crossing over create genetic variation.
sections.visual: Crossing over exchanges DNA between homologous chromosomes. Mutation changes a base. Assortment shuffles chromosomes.
sections.diagram: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 400" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Variation mechanisms"><title>Variation mechanisms</title><rect x="0" y="0" width="800" height="400" rx="16" fill="#101923"/><text x="28" y="35" fill="#e8ecf1" font-size="21" font-family="sans-serif">Variation comes from several mechanisms</text><path d="M28 51 L772 51" fill="none" stroke="#344253" stroke-width="2"/><text x="120" y="140" fill="#7cc7ff" font-size="16">Mutation</text><text class="lw-mut-base" x="120" y="180" fill="#ffd479" font-size="20">A→G</text><text x="320" y="140" fill="#7ee2a8" font-size="16">Crossing over</text><rect class="lw-xo-before" x="300" y="160" width="80" height="20" fill="#7cc7ff"/><rect class="lw-xo-after" x="300" y="200" width="80" height="20" fill="#b39dff"/><text x="560" y="140" fill="#b39dff" font-size="16">Assortment</text><circle class="lw-shuffle-a" cx="560" cy="190" r="12" fill="#7cc7ff"/><circle class="lw-shuffle-b" cx="600" cy="190" r="12" fill="#ffd479"/><path d="M28 350 L772 350" fill="none" stroke="#344253" stroke-width="2"/><text x="28" y="379" fill="#9aa6b8" font-size="15">Mechanism sketches · not trait predictions</text></svg>

questions.q: Name the three sources of genetic variation in this section.
questions.hint: One changes a base, one swaps segments, one shuffles whole chromosomes.
questions.answer: Mutation, crossing over, and independent assortment. Mutation changes a base; crossing over exchanges DNA between homologous chromosomes; assortment shuffles chromosomes.

questions.q: What does crossing over physically do?
questions.hint: It acts between a specific pair of chromosomes.
questions.answer: It exchanges DNA between homologous chromosomes, so each resulting chromosome carries a new combination of the parents' segments.

sections.heading: Genetics in the Wild
sections.body: Sequencing reads DNA order. Editing aims to change a chosen target.
sections.visual: Reading a sequence is different from editing it. Sequencing observes; editing intervenes at a target site.
sections.diagram: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 400" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Reading vs editing"><title>Reading vs editing</title><rect x="0" y="0" width="800" height="400" rx="16" fill="#101923"/><text x="28" y="35" fill="#e8ecf1" font-size="21" font-family="sans-serif">Reading a sequence is different from editing it</text><path d="M28 51 L772 51" fill="none" stroke="#344253" stroke-width="2"/><text x="120" y="150" fill="#7cc7ff" font-size="18">Sequence</text><text class="lw-seq-cursor" x="120" y="190" fill="#ffd479" font-size="16">ATCG…</text><text x="450" y="150" fill="#7ee2a8" font-size="18">Edit</text><text class="lw-edit-before" x="450" y="190" fill="#9aa6b8" font-size="16">before</text><text class="lw-edit-target" x="520" y="190" fill="#ffd479" font-size="16">TARGET</text><text class="lw-edit-after" x="620" y="190" fill="#9aa6b8" font-size="16">after</text><path d="M28 350 L772 350" fill="none" stroke="#344253" stroke-width="2"/><text x="28" y="379" fill="#9aa6b8" font-size="15">Conceptual comparison</text></svg>

questions.q: What is the difference between sequencing and editing DNA?
questions.answer: Sequencing reads the DNA order — it observes. Editing aims to change a chosen target in the sequence — it intervenes at a target site.

questions.q: Does sequencing a genome change it?
questions.hint: Reading versus intervening — which one is sequencing?
questions.answer: No. Sequencing only reads the order of bases. Changing a chosen target is editing, a different act.

questions.q: In DNA, the base C pairs with…
questions.explain: The pairings are A with T and C with G. The two backbones hold these complementary pairs.

questions.q: DNA stores its information in…
choices: The order of its base pairs
questions.explain: The body states it directly: DNA stores information in base pairs. The backbones are the holders; the sequence is the message.

questions.q: The central dogma path, as simplified in this course, runs…
questions.explain: DNA is transcribed to RNA; RNA is translated to protein. Proteins then help produce traits.

questions.q: Translation produces…
questions.explain: In this simplified path, a gene is transcribed into message RNA, then translated into a chain of amino acids — the protein.

questions.q: For an Aa × Aa cross under complete dominance, the phenotype ratio is…
questions.explain: Genotypes run 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa. Under complete dominance AA and Aa share the dominant phenotype, so phenotypes run 3:1.

questions.q: Each offspring in an Aa × Aa cross gets its two alleles…
questions.explain: Each cell of the Punnett square combines one allele from each parent — that is why four combinations are possible.

questions.q: A single base in a DNA sequence changes from A to G. That is an example of…
questions.explain: Mutation changes a base — the diagram's example is exactly A→G. Crossing over exchanges segments between homologous chromosomes, and assortment shuffles chromosomes.

questions.q: Crossing over creates variation by…
questions.explain: Crossing over exchanges DNA between homologous chromosomes, producing new combinations along the chromosome — different from mutation, which changes a base.

questions.q: A lab reports the full base order of a patient's gene without altering it. The lab performed…
questions.explain: Sequencing reads DNA order — it observes. Editing is the act that aims to change a chosen target.

questions.q: Editing differs from sequencing because editing…
choices: Aims to change a chosen target in the sequence
questions.explain: The section contrasts the two directly: sequencing observes; editing intervenes at a target site to change it.

sections.title: Four letters, two pairings
bullets: DNA stores information in base pairs.
A pairs with T; C pairs with G.
Two sugar-phosphate backbones hold the complementary pairs.
sections.notes: Everything in genetics starts as text. Four bases, two strict pairings, and the order along the backbones is the stored information.
sections.visual: The two sugar-phosphate backbones hold complementary base pairs: A with T, C with G.

sections.title: DNA → RNA → protein
bullets: Transcription: DNA is copied into RNA.
Translation: RNA is read to build a chain of amino acids.
sections.notes: The central dogma in one line: the gene is transcribed into a message, the message is translated into a protein, and proteins do the work that shows up as traits.
sections.visual: In this simplified path, a gene is transcribed into message RNA, then translated into a chain of amino acids.

sections.title: One cross, two ratios
bullets: Each offspring gets one allele from each parent.
Aa × Aa genotypes: 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa.
sections.notes: Count the allele combinations first — 1:2:1 — then let dominance merge AA and Aa into one visible phenotype for the 3:1.
sections.visual: Each cell combines one allele from each parent. Genotype ratio 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa.

sections.title: Three sources of variation
bullets: Crossing over exchanges DNA between homologous chromosomes.
sections.notes: Variation is manufactured three ways: edit a letter, swap segments between paired chromosomes, or shuffle which chromosomes travel together.
sections.visual: Crossing over exchanges DNA between homologous chromosomes. Mutation changes a base. Assortment shuffles chromosomes.

sections.title: Reading is not editing
bullets: Sequencing reads the order of DNA — it observes.
Editing aims to change a chosen target — it intervenes.
sections.notes: Modern genetics runs on the difference between these two acts: reading a sequence tells you what is written; editing reaches in and changes a chosen target.
sections.visual: Reading a sequence is different from editing it. Sequencing observes; editing intervenes at a target site.

enrichment.audioTitle: Genetics: The Code That Builds You — a conversation

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Four letters run this whole course. In DNA, what pairs with A, and what pairs with C?

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: A pairs with T, and C pairs with G.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: And where is the information — in the sugar-phosphate backbones, or somewhere else?

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: In the order of the base pairs the backbones hold. The backbones are the shelving; the sequence is the text.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Good image. Now the path from gene to trait — name the two steps.

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: Transcription makes RNA from DNA, then translation builds a chain of amino acids — a protein — from the RNA. Proteins help produce traits.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: The central dogma, simplified. Next: two carriers, Aa × Aa. Predict the ratios.

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: Genotypes 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa, and with complete dominance the phenotypes go 3:1.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Where does each allele in those squares come from?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Now variation. A base flips from A to G in one generation. Which mechanism is that, and how do the other two differ?

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: That is mutation. Crossing over swaps DNA between homologous chromosomes, and independent assortment shuffles which chromosomes go together.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Last distinction: a clinic sequences a patient's gene. Has the clinic changed the patient's DNA?

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: No — sequencing reads the order; it observes. Changing a chosen target would be editing.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Reading versus intervening. Hold those apart and the headlines about genetics get much easier to judge.
